month.title: Start small, build the habit
month.theme: Set up a safe practice loop: HTML, CSS, Git, and a first useful page.
month.mastery: Semantic page without a tutorial · recreate a design in HTML/CSS · recover a broken branch · explain the browser
month.checkpoint: A live page, a clean repo with real commits, four weekly reviews. Can you change the page without a tutorial, and explain what the browser is doing?

weeks.title: HTML foundations
weeks.objective: Write a semantic HTML page from a blank file and know why every element is there.
learn: How a browser turns an HTML file into a page (the DOM tree)
Document structure: doctype, html, head, body, meta viewport
Semantic landmarks: header, nav, main, section, article, footer
Headings as an outline; paragraphs, lists, links, images with alt text
Forms: label, input types, button, accessible names
Your workshop: editor, browser DevTools Elements panel, file and folder hygiene
practice: Mark up a recipe from a cookbook photo using only semantic elements
Open 3 sites you admire in DevTools and sketch their landmark structure
Write a contact form where every input has a label; complete it using only Tab and Enter
Run a page through the W3C validator and fix every error

build.title: Personal profile page
build.brief: A one-page profile: who you are, what you design, three pieces of work, and a contact form. HTML only this week; styling comes in Week 2. Structure first.

weeks.prove: Mastery test: build a semantic page from a blank file with no tutorial open.
reflect: Which element did you reach for out of habit (a div?) and replace with something meaningful?
weeks.ship: Profile page saved in a project folder you will push to GitHub in Week 3, and opened by one other person on their device.

tryFirst.task: Mark up a navigation bar with three links (Work, About, Contact) so that a screen reader announces it as navigation.
tryFirst.hint: There is an element whose whole job is 'this is a group of navigation links'. Lists are also announced with their item count.
tryFirst.explanation: Landmark elements (header, nav, main, footer) let assistive technology jump between regions. A nav containing a list is announced as 'navigation, list, 3 items': structure a pile of divs can't express.

weeks.title: CSS fundamentals
weeks.objective: Turn structure into a designed, responsive page, and understand the layout engine instead of nudging pixels.
learn: The cascade, specificity and inheritance
The box model: content, padding, border, margin, box-sizing
Typography on the web: font stacks, rem, line-height, measure
Flexbox for one-dimensional layout
Grid for two-dimensional layout
Responsive design: fluid widths, media queries, clamp()
Custom properties (CSS variables) as design tokens
Focus states and colour contrast
practice: Recreate a type scale from one of your Figma files using rem and custom properties
Play Grid Garden, then build the same layouts again from memory
Make a card component that reflows from 1 to 2 to 3 columns
Find what causes horizontal scroll at 375px using DevTools, and fix it

build.title: Responsive landing page
build.brief: A landing page for a real or imagined studio service. Design it in Figma first, then build it. It must work from 375px to 1440px with no horizontal scroll.

weeks.prove: Mastery test: recreate a reference design using only HTML and CSS.
reflect: Where did your Figma design and the browser disagree, and who was right?
weeks.ship: Landing page viewable on your phone, with screenshots at 375px and 1440px.

tryFirst.task: Make a row of three cards that sit side by side on desktop and stack on phones, without writing a media query.
tryFirst.hint: Grid can decide the number of columns itself if you tell it the minimum width a card may have.
tryFirst.explanation: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)) asks the browser to fit as many columns of at least 240px as the container allows, then share out the leftover space. The layout responds to its container, not to device breakpoints.

resources.title: CSS-Tricks · A complete guide to Flexbox

weeks.title: Git and GitHub
weeks.objective: Put your work under version control and on GitHub, so your history becomes evidence and your mistakes become recoverable.
learn: Repositories: what Git tracks and what it ignores (.gitignore)
Commits: staging, and writing messages that explain why
Branches: working on a change without touching main
Pull requests: proposing and reviewing a change
README: the front door of a project
Version history: log, diff, revert, restore
practice: Complete the Introduction sequence on Learn Git Branching
Make 5 small commits to your profile page with messages a stranger would understand
Create a branch, change the hero copy, open a pull request to yourself, and merge it
Delete a file on purpose, commit, then recover it from history

build.title: Put an actual project on GitHub
build.brief: Push your Week 2 landing page to a GitHub repository with a README covering what it is, a screenshot, how to run it, and what you learned. Turn on GitHub Pages if the repository is public.

weeks.prove: Mastery test: recover from a deliberately broken branch.
reflect: What would have been lost before this week if your laptop had died?
weeks.ship: Repository URL with at least 5 meaningful commits, one merged pull request, and a README.

tryFirst.task: You committed a change that broke the page. Undo it without deleting history.
tryFirst.hint: There is a command that creates a new commit which is the exact opposite of an old one.
tryFirst.explanation: git revert <commit> adds a new commit that undoes a previous one. History stays honest: anyone can see what happened and why. git reset rewrites history and is dangerous on shared branches.
tryFirst.solution:
git log --oneline     # find the bad commit, e.g. a1b2c3d
git revert a1b2c3d    # creates an 'undo' commit
git push

weeks.title: Web fundamentals + first mini-project
weeks.objective: Understand what happens between typing a URL and seeing a page, and ship a complete page that proves it.
learn: URL to DNS to HTTP request to response: the journey of a page
How the browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM
Render tree, layout and paint, and why some CSS is expensive
Where JavaScript runs and how it changes the DOM
DevTools: Network, Elements and Console panels
Performance basics: image sizes, fonts, Lighthouse
practice: Open the Network panel on 3 sites; note request count, page weight and the slowest file
Add 10 lines of JavaScript that toggle a menu, and watch the DOM change in Elements
Run Lighthouse on your landing page and fix the top 3 issues
Draw the URL-to-pixels journey from memory

build.title: A complete responsive webpage
build.brief: Extend your landing page into a small complete site: 2–3 sections, a working mobile menu (a few lines of JS), optimised images, a Lighthouse accessibility score of at least 95, deployed on GitHub Pages or Netlify.

weeks.prove: Mastery test: explain how browser, HTML, CSS and JavaScript work together, using your own site.
reflect: Which part of the URL-to-pixels journey was invisible to you before this week?
weeks.ship: Live URL on a free host, linked from the README, plus a Lighthouse screenshot.

tryFirst.task: Your page shows a menu button on mobile, but tapping it does nothing. Make it open and close the navigation.
tryFirst.hint: Find the button and the nav in JavaScript, listen for a click, and flip something the CSS can respond to. Also tell assistive technology whether the menu is open.
tryFirst.explanation: JavaScript shouldn't style things directly. It changes state (a class or an attribute) and CSS reacts. aria-expanded keeps the visual state and the accessible state in sync.

mastery.title: Semantic webpage from a blank file
mastery.challenge: Build a semantic webpage about a topic you know well (your design process, a city, a craft), starting from an empty file.
constraints: No copy-paste from other pages; looking things up on MDN is allowed
HTML only (minimal CSS allowed); no frameworks
criteria: Uses header, nav, main, footer and at least two sections with headings
Heading levels form a correct outline with no skipped levels
Every image has meaningful alt text (or empty alt if decorative)
Every form control has a visible label and can be reached with Tab
Passes the W3C validator with no errors
You can explain why each landmark element exists

mastery.title: Recreate a reference design in HTML/CSS
mastery.challenge: Pick a reference screen (a landing section from a site you admire, or one of your own Figma frames) and recreate it using only HTML and CSS.
constraints: Only HTML and CSS: no frameworks, no UI kits, no JavaScript
Don't copy the reference site's source; inspect it only for measurements
criteria: Close visual match at desktop width (overlay a screenshot to check)
Works at 375px with no horizontal scroll
Uses custom properties for colour, spacing and type
Layout uses Flexbox/Grid, not absolute-positioning hacks
Visible focus state on every interactive element
You can explain each layout decision

mastery.title: Recover from a broken branch
mastery.challenge: On a feature branch, three commits break the page and one good change is buried among them. Recover a working main branch that keeps the good change.
constraints: Command line or GitHub Desktop are both fine, but you must explain each step
No deleting and re-cloning the repository
criteria: main works correctly at the end
The good change is preserved
History shows what happened (revert or cherry-pick, not erased)
Every command you ran is written down with the reason
You can explain the difference between revert, reset and restore

mastery.title: Explain the browser pipeline
mastery.challenge: Explain, out loud or in writing and without notes, how the browser turns a URL into an interactive page, using your own deployed site as the example.
constraints: No notes or slides while explaining; a blank sheet for drawing is fine
Use your own site's Network panel as evidence
Record it (voice memo or screen recording) or write it in 600 words or fewer
criteria: Covers request, response, HTML parsing, DOM/CSSOM, layout and paint
Explains where and when JavaScript runs and how it changes the DOM
Points at one real request in your Network panel and explains its status, size and timing
Names one performance improvement you made and why it helped
Someone non-technical could follow it
